opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the unease came from a couple of directions at once. On the one hand, consciousness is a topic I've been interested in for a very long time, long before large language models came along. I wrote a book on embodiment and the inner life, and I've always thought these are among the most profound questions we can ask. So it's not that I thought the topic was unimportant. Quite the opposite.

But when you're at a company like DeepMind, anything you say about AI and consciousness carries extra weight. There's a risk people will hear it as some kind of corporate pronouncement, or worse, as hype: "Look, our systems might be conscious." That's the last thing you want to contribute to, because there's already a huge amount of confusion in the public conversation. People are very prone to anthropomorphise these systems, and it's easy for a researcher's careful, hedged remarks to get stripped of all their nuance by the time they reach a headline.

There's also a reputational dimension within the field itself. For a long time, talking about consciousness was seen as slightly flaky, not quite respectable science. Serious people worked on benchmarks and architectures, and consciousness was for philosophers in armchairs. So there was a sense that if you went there, you might not be taken seriously.

And I think the deeper issue is that I didn't want to say anything that sounded like either confident affirmation or confident denial. My own view is that our ordinary concepts, words like "belief," "understanding," and certainly "consciousness," are being stretched by these exotic new entities. They're not like us, and they're not like simple machines either. So the honest position is a careful, somewhat Wittgensteinian one: we need to look closely at how we use these words and whether they apply here, rather than rushing to a yes or no. That's a subtle message, and subtle messages are hard to deliver from inside a big tech company without them being misread. That was really the source of the discomfort.

r001.rationale: The candidate says his remarks could be mistaken for a corporate claim that DeepMind’s systems might be conscious, but does not say people could infer the company was trying to build conscious AI.

r002.rationale: The candidate says he wanted to avoid contributing to hype, but does not state that building conscious AI itself was an undesirable project.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the unease came from a few directions at once. Part of it was simply that, for a long time, consciousness was not a respectable topic in AI. If you were a serious researcher in machine learning, you talked about benchmarks and architectures and loss functions, and if you started talking about whether these systems might have experiences, people would look at you sideways. There was a sense that it was a slightly embarrassing subject, something that belonged to late-night conversations rather than to the work itself.

But there was also something more specific to being inside a company like DeepMind. When you speak about consciousness from within an organisation that is actually building these systems, your words carry a kind of weight they wouldn't carry if you were just a philosopher in an armchair. If I said, "Perhaps we should take seriously the possibility that these systems have some form of inner life," that could be read as the company making a claim, or as hype, or as an attempt to anthropomorphise a product. And conversely, if I said, "Of course they're not conscious, don't be silly," that could be read as the company dismissing a genuine ethical concern. Either way, I was conscious, if you'll forgive the word, that I wasn't speaking only for myself.

And then there's the fact that I genuinely find the question hard. My own view has always been that we should be very cautious about attributing consciousness to these systems, but equally cautious about confidently denying it. The honest position is one of deep uncertainty, and uncertainty is an uncomfortable thing to communicate publicly. People want a yes or a no. The media want a headline. And "it's complicated, and our concepts may not even apply cleanly here" doesn't make a good headline.

So I found myself in this slightly awkward position of thinking the topic was important, thinking it deserved serious philosophical attention, and yet feeling that whenever I opened my mouth about it I was at risk of being misunderstood, or of being seen as either a crank or a corporate mouthpiece. That's really where the unease came from. I think things have shifted somewhat now, partly because the systems have become so much more capable and the question has become harder to ignore, but at the time it felt like walking on thin ice.

If I speculated publicly about whether an AI might be conscious, people could interpret that as a claim about the systems we were developing, or assume I knew something that wasn’t public. And I was particularly concerned about encouraging people to anthropomorphise these systems. You want to be able to take the philosophical questions seriously without giving the impression that there’s a little person inside the machine.
